themes: Bristol clearance
Corner key

problems.note: REJECTED by E. Bourd: three white knights = promoted piece, a fatal flaw. Kept as the record of the mistake; the corrected setting is claude-bristol-corner. 1.Bh1! (2.Qg2#). The bishop must clear the whole a8-h1 diagonal for the queen AND keep protecting g2 (Qg2 unprotected is answered by Kxg2), so the far corner is the only square: 1.Ba6/Bc8? Kg1! and any nearer diagonal square blocks the queen. Black king boxed in the diagram (g1/g3 Se2, h1/g2 Bb7, h3 Sf2). 1...Sc6 (interposition, unguards f3) 2.Sf3#; 1...Sf3 (interposition) 2.Sxf3#; 1...h3 (self-block, attacks g2) 2.Sg4#; 1...f3 (interposition opening b8-h2) 2.Qb8#. Grown from the 5-unit kernel Q7/KB6/6N1/8/8/8/7k/8 (already sound). The pawn f4 is the b8-h2 blocker: only a pawn can open a line by interposing without being able to return (a knight or rook that interposes can step back onto the diagonal against Qb8+). Kc8 blocks the queen's 8th-rank routes (Qc8-h3, Qg8-g2, Qh8), Se1 blocks the first rank against Qa1, the d4 knight blocks the long diagonal against the same Qa1-h8. Flaws: Kc8 passive, three knights, Sf3/Sxf3 is the same mating square twice.

themes: Black correction

problems.note: Adjacent knight (bK c4, bS b5), built small and extended. The knight's departure gives the king b5, so every knight move defends against the threat; its error is leaving the b-file: 1.Re7! (2.Qg8#) S~ 2.Qb3#. Two self-block corrections by different motives: 1...Sd4 guards b3 and blocks d4, 2.Se5# (unmasking Ba8 on d5); 1...Sc3 cuts the f3 rook's protection of b3 and blocks c3, 2.Se3#. The same theme from White's side: the rook has no true random move; 1.Rh8? is the nearest and fails to Kd5! because e4 is lost; its 'aggressive corrections' 1.Re5? and 1.Ree3? (the latter cutting Rf3-c3) are each refuted by the corresponding black correction, Sd4! and Sc3!; 1.Re7! is the correction with no negative effect. Kd7+Bh3+f5+f4 stop 1.Re4+ (fxe4 is a discovered check) and its by-product 1...f4+; a3 stops Sb2+/Re5, Be1 stops Rd3/Rc3+/Re5. problems.note: Queen ambush behind the knight: 1.Qh5! (2.Qf7#). The knight's departure from f5 unmasks Qh3-e6 (so every knight move defends, Qe6 parries the threat) and opens h5-d5 for the random mate: S~ 2.Qd5#. The queen plays key, threat and all three mates, from an active post to the ambush. No tries worth the name (1.Qb1?/1.Qa1? both fail to Sxd4!), no changed mates, no duals; every unit load-bearing. 15 units. His reservation: Sd6 carries a double effect and Se3 a single one; in a symmetrical theme the thematic variations should be roughly equal in effect, so the imbalance is a drawback.

problems.note: 1.Rf1! (2.Rf8#). Both steps of the d7 pawn defend for one reason, the flight d7 (and 1...d6 also unprotects f8). Both mates use the vacated d7: 2.Qe6# is possible only because the pawn no longer guards e6, 2.Ba4# only because the a4-e8 diagonal is open. Each landing square closes exactly one white line: 1...d6 cuts Ba3-e7, so 2.Ba4+ fails to Ke7 and only 2.Qe6# mates; 1...d5 cuts the queen's road a2-d5-e6, so only 2.Ba4# mates. Flaws: plain key (rook to the open file), passive white king (it stops Re1 and Qe2), no set play for the thematic pair, Rb8 exists for the try and against 1.Ba4. His verdict (session 29): the play is not bad, with nice dual avoidance between two mates that both seem possible after any pawn move; 1.Rf1 is really bad, a piece out of play; a set-play change would need a whole new mechanism, not a few units.

problems.note: 1.Ke4! (zugzwang) c6 2.Sf5#, c5 2.Qh6#; try 1.Be6? c6 2.Sc8#, c5 2.Qxe5# but 1...e4!. Both steps are self-blocks, each on a square guarded by a different white piece: c6 was the knight e7's square (so the knight is released), c5 the queen's (e3-c5, so the queen is released). That gives the split of the mates between knight and queen. Try and key each do two things at once: 1.Be6 vacates c8 for Sc8 and closes the queen's 6th rank (no Qh6); 1.Ke4 vacates f5 for Sf5 and closes the queen's e-file (no Qxe5). In the set position both queen mates work after c5 (dual) and each phase kills one of them. His words: 'at first I just had two mates, then I somehow had to separate, that's obviously the hard part. Here it's square vacations and line changes for the queen. Not so simple geometrically.' Process (journal): 20 minutes on the d7/Ke6 setting found the pair of mates per step quickly; the selectors were bishop f6/d8 (knight mate) and king g5/f4 (queen mate), two different pieces, so no single move could switch both. He shifted the whole scheme one file left, after which one king move and one bishop move each carry both switches; he built the post-key position first (king on e4) and retracted the king to f5. The e5 pawn then refutes Be6 and cut the cooks from 11 keys to 4; wPd2 + bPd3 stop Qa3+, Qc3 and Qc1 (a search found no single unit that does it). Flaws: set play c6 and e4 unprovided, c5 set dual; the key takes the e4 move away from Black; zugzwang means the steps do not defend against anything; thin content (two variations, Black has two moves after the key); king key.

Re1 guards e5 (and e4 with Pf3); the threat Se7+ takes the knight's guard of e5 away, so the bishops defend by cutting the e-file on e2/e3, far from the king, which makes Kxe5 possible. Bb5 held c6, Bc5 held d6: Qxc6#/Qxd6#, and Qxd6 after Be2 or Qxc6 after Be3 is captured by the other bishop. Set play: Be3 Qxd6# set, Be2 unprovided (Kxe5 after Qxc6+), the key adds that mate. Every unit needed (trim); g5 stops the double threat Sf4#, Kc7 protects both mating queens. Gate PASS. Flaws: one try only (no try is refuted by Be3, since Qxd6 covers e5 itself); 7 pawns; Rc3 only guards c4; checking tries only otherwise. How he made it: scheme Kd5, Rh6, bishops c3/d3 cutting the 6th rank at f6/g6 (spread: line and cut squares away from the king); built the post-key with a knight threat; when the only key was the check 1.Rh4+ he moved the White king and queen, stripped Sa4, bQb1, bPb2, and turned the board a quarter (the black c2/c3/c4 chain that checked the king, captured on b3 and promoted became a static b6/c6/d6 chain, the targets of the mates); three changes later the post-key had no hole; findkey gave five unique keys (Sf8/Sh8/Sh4-g6, Rb3/Ra3-c3); he chose Sf8-g6 because f8 also gives the try Sh7?.

Bc6 leaves the d7 guard of e6, so after the key only Rh6 holds the e6 pawn; in the diagram the queen also holds it down the e-file, and the key gives that up. The bishops cut the 6th rank (Kxe6 after Bc6+); Bc3 held b4, Bc2 held b3; the other bishop's guard stops the dual. Gate PASS, trim-minimal. Flaws: g5 only stops 1.Rh5+, Kb8 passive (any of h1, g2, h2, a7, b8), Sa8 only stops the second threat Sc7#, d6 stops Be5 (a check on b8, and a guard of d6), set dual after Be4, tries 1.Kb7?/1.Bc8? both refuted by Bd3, 11+4. How he made it: scheme Rh6, Pe6, Bd7, Kd5, bishops c3/c2 (the threat square moved from d6 to e6, on the same line; the light bishop on c2 so its error lands on b3, away from the line); post-key Qb5 with Sa6, Pd6 (stops Be5); findkey: only key 1.Qf1-b5! His words: 'i left freedom in my geometry around the threat, and what squares could be needed... i changed the mates with the bishops, putting them away from the line, they are less interfering with other play and dont need a lot of patching'. His point (11 Oct): 'both mating pieces guard the same c5... each of the other variations they have a job, in some kind of mutual work of who guards c5. this way the play seems connected, and not like 2 distant variations'. The key makes c5 guarded twice (Sa6 -> Qb5,Sa6); after Bf6 the queen alone holds it for Sb4#, after Bg6 the knight alone for Qb3#.

Defence motive: the threat 2.Sb7# unmasks Rc1 (c7, c8) and cuts Ba6-c8 itself; the self-block on c7 also cuts the c-file, so c8 would be free
Mutual dual avoidance: the knight on c7 guards e8 (no 2.Qe8), the bishop on c7 guards b8 (no 2.Rb8); 1...Sc7 also cuts the bishop's guard of b8

Flaws: no tries (the key knight is the only unit that can cover d7 and protect e8, so no try pair by it); Ng5 only guards e6 against a second threat 2.Se6#, Ph6 only protects it (stops 1.Qxg5+); Kd3 takes part in no mate (stops cooks); Ba6 is in no mate (guards c8: without it 1...Kc8 refutes and the diagram has a flight); random-move duals after Ng5 moves (Sb7#/Se6#); the Sc7 mate is already set. Not anticipated by the gate; the capture form (sacrifice captured by K, S, B on one square) is Strebkovs, Vratnica-64 2003 (psis-fd6a6d0ccf) and Muralidharan 2002, so the self-blocks here are on an empty square. Found by: freethreat/postsearch (SELFBLOCK=1), then on the edge (Kd8: five field squares instead of eight at d5), unmask_search KSQ f6 FSQ d5 and a hand change of the key's start (d5 -> e8: on d5 it protected e7, giving 1.Be7#). E. Bourd (12 Oct 2026): 'your mechanism is mega complicated, and you made it. the key is nice giving flight, the position is generally ok, with the b2 rook only being active in 1 variation. other than that pretty impressive honestly. you went into very hard constructions to achieve it. using the flight mechanism of self-block.' problems.source: black half-pin of a rook and a knight on a diagonal (basic scheme, no tries)
themes: Black half-pin on the diagonal b1-e4: Bb1 x-rays Rc2 and Sd3 to Ke4; on a diagonal the pinned unit cannot move at all
Both thematic defences guard the threat square d5: 1...Sf4 and 1...Rc5
Knight variation: 2.Qc4# (the pinned rook cannot take on c4)
Rook variation: 2.Qg4# (the pinned knight cannot block on f4)
Dual avoidance by the arrival squares: Sf4 blocks the 4th rank (no Qg4), the rook on c5 still holds c4 (no Qc4)
Flight-giving key: d4
problems.note: 1.Qh8-g8! (2.Qd5#) Sf4 2.Qc4#, Rc5 2.Qg4#; 1...Kd4 2.Qd5#. Gate PASS, 7+5. Built by colour reasoning: the knight on d3 covers dark squares only, so its pin mates are line mates through e5/f4 (4th rank from the east: Qg4), and its arrival must spoil the other mate (f4 blocks the 4th rank); the rook's pin mate is a line mate through c4 (Qc4), spoiled after 1...Rc5 because the rook keeps its file. d4 must stay unguarded after the key: with d4 guarded, 1...Rc5 also allowed 2.Bxd3# (the pinner takes the pinned knight, d3 protected) and the queen's checks Qg6+/Qh7+ mated; the free d4 makes the key give a flight. Units: Bh6 e3/f4 (without it 1.Qg8 fails to 1...Rxd2); Pd2 c3/e3 and blocks the rook's 2nd rank (no Rg2+); Kg3 f3/f4; Sd7 e5; Se7 d5/f5; bPb4 stops 1.Bxc2 (zugzwang) and the third defence 1...Sb4; bPd6 stops 1.Be3. Flaws: no tries, no set play, both defences merely guard the threat square, three soundness units (bPb4, bPd6, Bh6), one mating unit (the queen) and no links between the variations.

His structure: Se3 on a field square holds d5/f5 and protects c4/g4 (replaces Se7, Bh6, Ra5); Sg6 guards e5/f4 and closes the g-file, which is the refutation mechanism of 1.Qg8. Rc5 is not 2.Qxd3#/Bxd3# (the pinned-knight capture); Pf2 holds e3 against 1...Rxd2 (without it the tries are lost) and fixes bPf3, so bBd1 is needed against 1.Bxc2 (recaptures); bPb4 stops 1...Sb4 (second knight defence, same Qc4#); Kh4 takes part in no mate (cook-stopper by position). Tested: one bSe1 for Sc1+Bd1 fails to 1...Sg2+ (Kh4) and to 5th-rank checks with Kh5.

1...Sf7 2.Qf2# (the pinned d5 knight cannot block on f4); 1...Se7 2.Qd7# (the pinned e5 knight cannot take on d7)
Dual avoidance by black line opening: Se5 leaves and bRe1 reaches e6 (Qd7+? Re6); Sd5 leaves and bBa8 reaches f3 (Qf2+? Bf3)
Set 1...R~ 2.Rxe5#, 1...Re4 2.dxe4#; no flight

Flaws: the key piece is attacked by Sd5 (1...Sxc7 has no set mate), milder than it looks (E. Bourd, 14 Oct 2026: 'key is slightly less flawed here, as we have a set mate, and the bishop seems to guard e5 as well'): on c7 the bishop is the only guard of e5 in the set 1...R~ 2.Rxe5# (seven rook moves) and doubles e5/f4 in the set 1...Sf7 2.Qf2#; c7 is the only free square that guards e5 and reaches d8 (b6 does not guard e5, e7 already guards f6, f6/g5 are occupied), so the attack follows from a set-play job and the key gives up that set mate; both tries fall to the same non-thematic hxg5; 20 units (8 pawns); Kb3 passive; random-move duals. (2.Qxd4#) cxd3!, 1.Qf7? (zugzwang, the solution's mates) h4!, 1.Bh3? h4!. Gate PASS, 7+5, trim: nothing removable. Units: Sf6 guards e4/d5 and blocks the queen's 6th rank (no Qe6 in the set); Bd7 guards f5/e6; Be7 d6 in the set and blocks the e-file (2.Qe8 after the key); Pe3 d4/f4; Pg5 shuts the g-file (Qg5, Qg3); bPc4 guards d3 (1.Qd3); bPh5 guards g4 (2.Sg4 would double 2.Qe4 after Sd5 and 2.Qd5 after Se4) and its tempo h4 refutes the waiting tries. problems.note: Gate PASS, 8+9, trim: nothing removable; an economy search (evolve type-1 mode with a candidate list) found no version under 17 units (Kd8 works as well as Kb8). By-play 1...Rd5 2.Qxd5# (the rook interferes with the queen's guard of e4; mate captures the defender on a thematic square). Flaws: six black cook-stoppers (Sa2 stops 1.Qb4# and the set Qc3; Rc1 stops 1...Sc1 and c1=S; Pc2 stops Bc2; Pb5 stops Rb5; Pf4 stops 1.Qe3#; Pg4 stops 1.Sf3+ Ke4 2.Qd3#), wKb8 closes the 8th rank (Qh8 checks), random-move duals (1...Bf5 2.Qd5#/Sb3#), long key into the corner. problems.author: Claude (24 Oct 2026, request 'two black knights defend on the same square')
problems.source: Hand scheme (Ke5, Sc7/Sg5 -> e6, Qd3 behind the threat knight d4) -> unmask_search KSQ=e2/b3/c2/b5 (claude-two-knights-e6-sb3 stage) -> second layer by hand: Rf6's 6th-rank guard of d6 through e6, key square f5 (the only landing guarding d6 that Black cannot take with a knight) -> unmask_search CORE Ke5/Sc7/Sg5/pf3/Qd3/Rf6/Sf5, EMPTY=e6,d6, TRIES d4->b3/e6 refuted by g5e6. Trim and four improvement runs: nothing better.
themes: Two black knights defend on the same square e6 (guard d4 against 2.Qd4#); departure selects the mate: 1...Sce6 (d5 unguarded) 2.Qd5#, 1...Sge6 (the e4 interposer gone) 2.Qe3#; each sibling mate fails to the knight that stayed (2.Qd5+? Sxd5, 2.Qe3+? Se4)
White correction: 1.S~ (b3, c2, e6) threatens 2.Qd4# but 1...Sge6! (the arrival on e6 cuts Rf6 from d6: 2.Qe3+ Kd6); 1.Se6? Scxe6 2.Qd5# but 1...Sgxe6!; 1.Sxb5? Sxb5+!; correction 1.Sf5! guards d6
Set: 1...Sh7/Sf7/Sh3 2.Qe3# (random g5 moves); 1...Sge6 has no set mate (the same e6 cut)
problems.note: Sound, 13 units (6+7, 3 pawns), gate PASS, trim: nothing removable. The common arrival effect (the e6 block cutting the 6th rank) is what refutes the random tries, and the key is the landing that re-guards the cut square d6. Flaws: no try is refuted by 1...Sce6 alone (no pure pair; the only landing that cuts a line 2.Qd5# needs is f5, the key, and a rook guarding f4 through f5 mates on f5 in the diagram); 1...gxf5 2.Rxf5# (bPg6 stops 1.Sxf3+, 1.Sc6+ and the S~ tries from solving, removal test); cook-stoppers Ka7 (1.Sxb5? Sxb5+! only), bBb5 (Sc6#, Re6+, and the b5 square), bPg4 (Sxf3+, Qe3+), bPf3 (2.Qe2# duals after Sge6/Sf3); random-move duals after the knights' non-defending moves (1...Se8 Qd5#/Qd4#); set Sce6/Sge6 unprovided. Level: medium (two thematic variations with one dual-avoidance motive plus a white correction).

problems.author: Claude (25 Oct 2026), theme set by E. Bourd ('two black knights defend on the same square')
problems.source: freethreat on the core Ke8/Se4/bSc4/bSg4 (WANT Sce5->Sd6#, Sge5->Sf6#, NOFLIGHT): the edge king boxed by Qc7 (d7, d8, e7) and Kg7 (f7, f8), threat Bh7-g6#; also found with Bg8 (threat Bf7#) and with Ke6+Pe7 as the box (4k3/4P2B/3pK2p/8/2n1N1n1/8/8/8, 7 units)
themes: Two black knights defend on the same square e5 by guarding the threat square g6; the mates are separated by the departures: c4 leaves d6 unguarded (2.Sd6#), g4 leaves f6 unguarded (2.Sf6#); 1...Sce5 2.Sxd6#, 1...Sge5 2.Sf6#

No key found: the threat bishop mates from every square it could come from (f5, g8, e6, d5), the box queen cannot move, the king cannot (Kg6 is checked by Sxe5+, Kg8 by Sh6+); keyfind, three diagsearch and eight evolve runs gave only flight-taking, capturing or zugzwang keys
problems.note: Sound post-key, 9 units (4+5), dual avoidance unified. Why no key (see lessons 25 Oct 2026): a rook unblocking g6 always has Rf6 with the second threat Rf8# (any White cover of f8 protects a rook there); a knight on g6 has six unblocking moves and Black has no refutation of the random ones (every defence against Bg6# is a knight move to e5); a rook or queen threat on d7/f7 along a file carries Rd8#/Rf8#. A try that blocks d6 is refuted twice (1...Sxd6 lands where it guards f7); one that blocks f6 is single (1...Sxf6 2.Sxf6#) but no piece on the f-file reaches f6 by a diagonal.

problems.author: Claude (25 Oct 2026), on E. Bourd's bench frame mvmxfkoj step 117 (Ke4, Sb5 pinned to Ka5 by Rf5, Rf5 pinned by Bh7)
problems.source: His step 117 (1B6/7B/4p2q/KN3rp1/2PPk3/5n1r/2P1NPP1/8): threat 2.Se2-c3#, 1...e5 2.Sbc3#, 1...Se5 2.Sd6#, six holes after the other moves of Sf3. Those moves open Rh3 to c3, so they defend: a Black correction without its mate. Pd4 removed, White queen on the long diagonal (2.Qd4#), black Sd7 guards e5 so that 2.Qxe5 fails after the correction; Rh3 -> Qh3 and Qh6 -> Rh6 for legality (corr1/corr2/diag scratch searches, by hand after that).
themes: Black correction: 1...S(f3)~ (opens h3-c3, defends against 2.Se2-c3) 2.Qd4#, 1...Sxd4 2.Qxd4#; 1...Sfe5! (unpins Sb5, cuts the queen at e5) 2.Sd6#

Two units interpose on e5 and unpin the knight; each departure opens a black line onto the other mating square: 1...e5 (h6-d6) 2.Sbc3#, 1...Sfe5 (h3-c3) 2.Sd6#; both cut Bc7-f4, so Se2 must stay: the threat's square c3 is taken by the other knight
A third unit on e5: 1...Sde5 2.Sd6#/Sbc3# (dual)
problems.note: Scheme, no key. Flaws: the dual after 1...Sde5 (the black guard of e5 must be a knight here, and a knight that guards e5 can always go there); 10+8. The cure, Rd8 behind the d7 knight (1...Sde5 then opens the d-file to d6, 2.Sbc3# only), needs a fourth black rook or queen: f5 pinner, 3rd rank, 6th rank, d-file - promoted. 3r4/p1Bn2QB/4p2r/KN3rp1/2P1k3/5n1r/2P1NPP1/8 is sound with Sde5 2.Sbc3# but has four rooks (illegal); with Bf8+Pe7 for the 6th rank the e7 pawn guards d6 (fails).
